title: What If Family Game Night Got Your Kids Talking About Scripture?
summary: What would it take to make a Bible game they’d ask to play again? That's the question Doxa Games asks. If your family is getting together this Christmas, pick a game, clear a spot at the table, and let the kids make the first move.  See Also Free Stuff Fridays (Harvest House Publishers) Free Stuff Fridays (Harvest House) The Hard Work Is Done—Family Bible Study Is Fun
content: This week, the blog is sponsored by Doxa Games . This post is written by Marco Bartholomae, founder of Doxa Games and creator of the Bible-based board and card games Trials & Triumphs , Bible Clash , and Hurry! Fleeing Disciples . A couple of years ago, I was playing cards with my kids when a question hit me. What would it take to make a Bible game they’d ask to play again? I grew up in Germany with four brothers. We played cards on long car rides and spent hours on our bedroom floor with a board game spread out between us. I still remember how easy it was to lose track of time when we played together. Now I live in California with my wife and our four children, and we still love a good game night. The screens go away, somebody wants a rematch, and we get to enjoy being together. That question from the card table stayed with me. I started imagining games that could give other families that same experience and get them talking about Scripture along the way, games a child could sit down to, learn the rules, and enjoy right away, even if they were new to the Bible. Then maybe a name on a card or something that happened on the board would make them curious enough to ask a question. That’s how Doxa Games started. The Conversations That Start Around the Table In Deuteronomy 6, God tells his people to speak about his commandments with their children as they go about ordinary life, including when they sit at home. A game night gives us another chance to do that. Our games don’t replace family devotions, but they do open conversations about God’s Word. Your child might pick up a card and ask who Thaddaeus was. A race to a house church might get them wondering why the early Christians gathered in homes. Those are questions you can follow right back to Scripture. That’s also why I chose the name Doxa . It’s the Greek word for glory . In 1 Corinthians 10:31, Paul reminds us to do everything to the glory of God, even in ordinary things like eating and drinking. That conviction shapes what we make and how we think about time around the table. Three Games to Play With Your Family Bible Clash: Gospels (ages 8+) is a fast-paced, head-to-head card game. Play characters from the four Gospels and try to outscore your opponent. Trials & Triumphs (ages 5+) sends players down a winding path where one turn can move you forward, and the next can set you back. It gives younger kids a way to talk about trusting Christ through trials. Hurry! Fleeing Disciples (ages 8+) takes you into the world of Acts. Choose your route, evade Roman guards, and race to reach a house church. From Our Family Table to the Mission Field As Doxa grows, we hope to translate these games and put them in the hands of missionaries, church planters, and ministry training centers in places like Colombia, the Philippines, and East Africa. I’d love for a family in Malawi to pull out one of these games, play it in their own language, and have the same kinds of conversations we have around our table. If your family is getting together this Christmas, pick a game, clear a spot at the table, and let the kids make the first move. See all three games at DoxaGames.com . title: The Empty Chair, the Ache, the Tear
summary: Six years after Nick died, his possessions still fill three bins in our basement. Twice a year I see them and am thankful for what they represent and what they make me long for. See Also Free Stuff Fridays (Harvest House Publishers) A Slave to Sin Captivity
content: Those who live in a cold-weather climate will be familiar with the twice-yearly ritual of swapping summer clothes for winter and winter clothes for summer. Sometime around November, we pull the clear Rubbermaid bins from their shelves in the basement, then unpack the toques, 1 gloves, fleece-lined boots, and heavy coats before repacking them with the out-of-season raincoats, baseball caps, running shoes, and sandals. We reverse the ritual in April or May—whenever we have finally enjoyed the kind of consistent warmth that heralds the arrival of spring and the coming of summer. It took some time after our son Nick’s death before we could clean out his room and begin to either dispose of his possessions or give them away. There were many we could not bring ourselves to purge, so we packed them into that same style of bin and stacked them on those same shelves. Now, twice a year I find myself catching glimpses of the bits and pieces of his life. To anyone else, these bins might seem to contain a random collection of clothes, gadgets, and paraphernalia, yet we associate every one of them with him. There’s a piggy bank shaped like a safe whose bell would ring whenever the girls playfully attempted to pillage it. There’s a selection of books that he read and reread: Tintin , Calvin & Hobbes , and a few volumes considerably more serious. There’s a sweater that looked especially handsome on him and, of course, his ever-present Blue Jays hat . There’s nothing of any real value, yet it’s invaluable to us. It’s a life reduced to three 14-gallon bins. I expect those bins will still be stacked on the shelves when Aileen and I die or need to move out of our home. I expect they will have all the same objects in them. We have learned that what is not purged immediately is likely to be kept indefinitely, for our attachment has only grown through the years. To throw them out or to give them away seems more disloyal today than it would have been six years ago . In fact, we can barely even allow ourselves to open those bins or to touch their contents. It’s just too painful to come into contact with all these things that remind us of a person who was once so much a part of our lives. Nick still is a part of our lives, I suppose, but in a different way. He’s no longer the son who delights us with his wit and impresses us with his brilliance. He’s no longer the son who checks in with Aileen when I’m traveling far from home or who is on call when I have questions about Greek or Hebrew. He’s the empty chair during the holidays, the ache when I think of happier times, the tear that springs to my eyes when we stand in church to sing of the future . He’s the lump in my throat when I consider Christ’s return and the joy that thrills my heart when I ponder heaven. He’s present still, but in a way that is as different as day is from night and pleasure is from pain. I’m thankful that we kept these items, these traces of his existence and reminders of what he used, wore, and enjoyed. I’m thankful that in their own way they remind me of him and all the joy he brought to our lives. I’m grateful that they cause me to long for the day when we leave them all behind, probably still in those Rubbermaid bins, and depart this world as Nick did—with nothing but the faith God has given us and the assurance that he will receive us. In that way, these valueless objects are immeasurably precious. Pronounced tewk (rhymes with duke ), this is a uniquely Canadian word for a winter hat (or what some refer to as a beanie). ↩︎ See Also Free Stuff Fridays (Harvest House Publishers) A Slave to Sin Captivity

content: Good morning. Grace and peace to you. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include some devotional and daily liturgy books like Dane Ortlund’s In the Lord I Take Refuge: 150 Daily Devotions through the Psalms and Jonathan Gibson’s Be Thou My Vision: A Liturgy for Daily Worship . Westminster Books has put together a Christmas Gift Guide that has all kinds of great options for anyone on your Christmas list. Recommended Reading Your Riches Are Stored Up in Leonida. Dakota Fiebranz says that since it’s the easiest and most expected thing in the world to criticize Grand Theft Auto , he takes a different tack and writes about what its popularity says about its users. “For those unfamiliar with the Grand Theft Auto series, the premise is relatively simple. You’re placed in a fictional American city, usually in the character of a criminal, and given a staggering amount of freedom to carry out your most dubious ambitions. You can steal cars (as the name suggests), but you can also rob banks, shoot civilians, commit vehicular manslaughter, and flee arrest, all with few to no consequences. You are truly free in the world of crime.” Learn From Autistic People About Evangelism. “These days, I seem to know an awful lot about trains. Train companies, liveries and logos. I know about engines and carriages, railway lines, stations and routes. I don’t actually use the trains all that much nor am I any sort of train enthusiast; I don’t, and never have, had any great interest in trains. What I am, however, is the father of a very classically autistic teenage boy.” Stephen Kneale explains what we can learn about evangelism from people with autism. How to Fire Someone at a Christian Organization. Unfortunately, even Christian people working for Christian organizations sometimes need to be let go. This article offers wisdom for those times. “When we hold back the hard call, we tell ourselves a story about mercy: I don’t want to be the one who upends this person’s life, so I won’t go there. That’s a heavy burden to put on your shoulders. To believe you’re ruining someone’s life by ending his employment is to believe you hold his future in your hands. But here’s the thing: You don’t. You aren’t sovereign over this person’s story. You cannot see his next chapter. The assumption that you can, that keeping him in a role where he’s failing is protecting him from some fate only you can foresee, isn’t humility. It’s pride.” America Needs a New Temperance Agenda. Brad Littlejohn writes about the recent political earthquake in the U.S. and explains why America needs a new temperance agenda. “Our markets, rather than serving American families, are tearing them apart, and American voters are primed for leaders willing to rein in an economy that caters to appetite and impulse rather than genuine human needs. Rather than narrowing our moral message, it’s time to broaden it—and with it, our coalition.” Praise God From Whom All Sparrows Flow. Kevin Burrell explains how a bird told him that the season of gratitude has begun. “The mid-fall arrivals of fall colors and flannel and pumpkin spice lattes can trigger our hearts to a sort of Thanksgiving nostalgia; they announce, like my backyard sparrows, ‘Remember, ‘tis the season to give thanks!’ But if we let them, these annual bellwethers can slingshot us well past an afternoon of turkey and football and reciting a couple of blessings around the table.” The Housing Crisis and the Biblical Duty of Stewardship. This is a thoughtful piece about the housing crisis. The context is the U.S., but much of it applies to Canada as well. “If we want young Americans to have a genuine opportunity to build stable lives, it’s not enough to implement another temporary affordability program. We need to recover a vision of economic life rooted in stewardship and responsibility, with the goal of flourishing families.” Reader Recommendations Once a week, I like to ask what you enjoy and recommend. title: Works & Wonders (November 22)
summary: This week’s Works & Wonders: NatGeo’s Pictures of the Year, Nubia’s great cathedral, satellites over your home, new music, and 200 million crabs. See Also Works & Wonders (November 15) Works & Wonders (Oct 11) Works & Wonders (September 27)
content: In my weekly Works & Wonders column, I combine a brief devotional with other interesting and uplifting bits and pieces I gleaned throughout the week. I hope you enjoy this week’s collection! It includes: God Can, God Does: A Devotional Pictures of the Year The Largest Cathedral Something Watched You Surely As the Morning 🎶 200 Million Crabs Heaven’s Refrain 🎶 1. God Can, God Does Theologians have long distinguished between what God can do and what God does do—between his absolute power and his ordained power. God’s absolute power is his ability to do whatever he pleases. There is no limit to what he can or could do. Hence, he could have created a second earth or several more moons. He could have created a world where the natural laws of gravity or relativity worked differently. He could have created a world without you or me. He could have wiped out humanity at the time of the Flood and been perfectly justified in doing so. He could have, but he did not. Hence, as George Swinnock says, “God does not do many things that He can”—many things that he has the ability to do. This is his absolute power, and it must be distinguished from his ordained power, the power God has actually chosen to exercise. God exercises his power in such a way that “He does all things that He will.” His power is such that he accomplishes all the things he desires and determines he will accomplish—with no man or woman, no force or creature, to hinder him or stand in his way. 2. Pictures of the Year I have linked to a bunch of photograph-of-the-year collections and competitions, but I’m quite sure none of them has been as incredible as National Geographic ‘s Pictures of the Year 2026 . They span a host of subjects, and it sometimes seems that each one is more amazing than the last. Enjoy them! 3. The Largest Cathedral We sometimes forget that some of the places in the world that are now inhospitable to the Christian faith were once much more welcoming to it. That is the case with modern-day Sudan, which was once known as Nubia. In Archaeologists reach the original floor of Nubia’s largest cathedral in Sudan , Archaeology News explains how a Sudanese-Polish team recently uncovered new sections of the Great Church of Jesus, known to be the largest and richest church in medieval Nubia—it’s around 47 meters wide, 57 meters long, and 21 meters high. Impressive! Adrian Chlebowski/ Polish Center of Mediterranean Archaeology, University of Warsaw 4. Something Watched You There are thousands of satellites in orbit around the Earth—reportedly, nearly 17,000 of them. With that being the case, it’s not surprising, I suppose, that something watched you this week. But what? Watched.earth has the answer. You can go to any place on Earth, see the satellites that have passed overhead recently, and in many cases, even see the photos they took. It’s both impressive and a little spooky! 5. Surely As the Morning I’ve often been surprised how few excellent renditions we have of Psalm 23, especially when so many people consider it the greatest of the Psalms. I was glad, then, to come across “ Surely As the Morning ” by The Wood Drake Sessions. It’s a faithful, toe-tapping rendition that I am very much enjoying. It’s part of the album East to West if you’d like to hear more from the group. 6. 200 Million Crabs The BBC is releasing some highlights of its new Blue Planet III documentary series, and this one is pretty impressive: 200 Million Crabs Reveal Extraordinary Behaviour Never Filmed Before . “In one of the largest crab gatherings ever recorded, millions of porcelain crabs form astonishingly orderly lines, working together to feast on plankton. But how do these tiny creatures coordinate on such an enormous scale? The answer remains a mystery. Witness this remarkable underwater phenomenon, captured on camera for the very first time in Blue Planet III .” It’s both amazing and bizarre! 7. summary: 40 great films for Christian parents to watch with their kids / Does the body really keep the score? / There’s no such thing as “your” weekend / To efficiency and beyond / What happens when schools ban phones / GTA 6 is pornographic and gory See Also Weekend A La Carte (December 27) Weekend A La Carte (November 30) Weekend A La Carte (May 25)
content: Good morning and welcome to Weekend A La Carte. Be sure to scroll down to read this week’s Reader Recommendations, since you will find some good and interesting ones there. And check in again tomorrow for Works & Wonders. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include some superb books like Kevin DeYoung’s Daily Doctrine and Mark Vroegop’s Waiting Isn’t a Waste . I have updated the Commentaries on Sale page. It includes deals in both print and Kindle editions, and you’ll find some great discounts there. Recommended Reading Brett McCracken watches a lot of movies, and that gives him the authority to create this list of 40 great films for parents to watch with their kids. In today’s glutted, morally compromised streaming-media environment, Christian families are right to worry about the countless options billed as “kid-friendly” but actually form kids in spiritually unhealthy ways. As a dad of four young kids, I know the struggle well. It’s impossible to keep up with the content conveyor belt of new film and TV options being marketed to kids. Christian parents need trusted curators who can reliably point us to entertainment that isn’t just “safe” for our kids to watch but is actively promoting laudable themes and (sometimes accidentally) modeling Christian virtue. This list is my attempt to help my fellow Christian parents in this struggle. The movies below are all G- or PG-rated and generally “safe for the whole family,” though parents should still consult online content guides to discern the appropriateness for their particular family. Read: 40 Great Films for Christian Parents to Watch With Their Kids. You’ve no doubt heard something about Bessel van der Kolk’s The Body Keeps the Score , a book that has been on the bestseller charts for more than 10 years. That book has done more than anything else to normalize a particular understanding of the relationship of the body to the mind and of the body’s response to trauma. Matthew Loftus, author of Resisting Therapy Culture explains why van der Kolk’s explanation is unsatisfying and no longer credible. As important as arguments over how to interpret scientific research are, the larger problem with pop theories of trauma has to do with misapplications of that research and outright misinformation. You may have seen ads, videos, or blog posts proclaiming that procrastination is a trauma response, a statement with no basis in scientific research but still accepted easily because it’s far easier to let go of one’s guilt over procrastination if it’s linked to trauma. The Canadian physician Gabor Maté argues that most mental illness is somehow linked to trauma—another baseless assertion that is nonetheless very popular. Expanding the definition of trauma can be powerful because it gives people a story that explains how they got to where they are—regardless of whether or not that story is true. We can’t always draw a hard-and-fast line to say “ this is psychological trauma” while “ that is just a very stressful experience” because stress and trauma are more of a continuum than two distinct categories. However, what we see now is an attempt to maximize the number of things considered as trauma, even using the language of “microtrauma.” Read: Does the Body Really Keep the Score? Since we have come to the weekend, perhaps you’d do well to be challenged by Zak Mellgren who wants you to know that it’s not “your” weekend. “How was your weekend?” I’ve used this phrases countless times myself. It is an ingrained, deeply rooted piece of my vocabulary. A conversation starter. A way to communicate interest in another person’s life. And let’s be clear up front, that is a wonderful thing. It is good to ask another image bearer about their daily life. “How was your weekend” opens the door to countless possible avenues of conversation. We will often get surface level small-talk from this question, but even these little details are worth our time. And we might get more than small-talk. We may learn of a doct

summary: It was a great honor to be able to partner with Missionary to create Goers, a series of illustrated biographies for children. content: It was a great honor to be able to partner with Missionary to create Goers , a series of illustrated biographies for children. Each biography introduces young readers and listeners to the stories of men and women who were sent by churches to spread the good news about Jesus Christ to the ends of the earth. Each is illustrated by the ultra-talented Rommel Ruiz. The books can be purchased as a set of three or as individual volumes. The Plowboy’s Bible: The Story of William Tyndale’s English Translation . Hunted by spies, William Tyndale fled across Europe with a bounty on his head, his Bible translation labeled as contraband. Young John, on the other hand, has a long day of farm work ahead of him. Although their lives seem worlds apart, John’s father knows a story that binds John and William together—their love for God’s word. The scripture John relies on for encouragement cost William everything, but they gave John’s family everything! Rescued from Darkness: Amy Carmichael and the Girls of Dohnavur . Kumari is scared, helpless, and alone in a dark temple until Amma, a mysterious woman from a faraway land, carries her away to a beautiful garden. This is not a fairy tale. It’s the true story of missionary Amy Carmichael and the children she rescued and raised at Dohnavur Fellowship in India. Into the Unknown: David Livingstone’s Heart for Africa . Before David Livingstone was the most famous man in the world, he was a boy who dreamed of being free to explore God’s creation. But when David reached the mission field, he found that freedom taken from the people he tried to teach about the Creator. This is the story of a goer’s dangerous journey to the ends of the earth, of his courageous stand for justice, and of his patient endurance for the sake of Christ. The Goers series is written for children ages 4–10, and is ideal for parents to read to their children or for young readers to read on their own. Each book includes discussion questions and prayer points to get your family thinking and praying about the Great Commission. Each hardcover volume has 40 full-color pages and is sized 10″ x 10″. The Goers series is currently available exclusively through Westminster Books . Look for three more volumes to be added to the series around this time next year. title: A La Carte (November 20)
summary: Wes Huff's plagiarism / Hot water and holy wonder / Are my prayers selfish? / When the heavens declare / Gospel-pilling the looksmaxxers / Lessons I’ve learned about single missionaries / Don’t be afraid to provoke your brothers / Kindle deals and more See Also A La Carte (April 1) A La Carte (March 7) A La Carte (Black Friday Edition)
content: Good morning. If you have read this site for any length of time, you will know that I am not the kind of person who does hot takes, since I just don’t trust myself to do them well. However, with the Wesley Huff situation developing, I did want to link to what I consider an especially helpful assessment of the matter. You can find that beneath today’s recommended reads. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include several volumes in the excellent New Studies in Dogmatics series. You’ll also find books by Jinger Duggar Vuolo, David Mathis, John Piper, and others. I continue to find and highlight hardcover and softcover book deals as part of Amazon’s Pre-Black Friday Book Deals . There are around 80 of them now, many of which are half off or more. Recommended Reading Hot Water and Holy Wonder: Giving Thanks for Ordinary Luxuries. “Every now and then, as I sit in my home library, a sense of awe settles over me—a spirit of wonder at the everyday comforts that surround me.” Trevin Wax celebrates the joy of the ordinary luxuries that God so graciously grants us. Are My Prayers Selfish? Responding to a question from a listener, John Piper explains the difference between prayers that are selfish and those that simply ask for things. “James is saying there is a kind of prayer that treats God like a cuckold. It refers to a husband whose wife is cheating on him. That’s a cuckold. Christians are making God into a cuckold. How? When it says they are praying just to spend it on their passions. The picture is of an unfaithful wife who asked her husband for $50 so she can go down the hall and pay another man to have sex with her. That’s the picture. She’s using prayer to cheat on her husband, God.” When the Heavens Declare: What a Solar Halo Says to a Secular City. Johannesburg was recently the site of a solar halo ( see here for images ). Tim Cantrell writes about what the skies were declaring in that moment. Gospel-Pilling the Looksmaxxers: Hope for Despairing Men. “What do dating apps, the 1999 film The Matrix, rhinoplasty, crystal meth, and smashing your face with a hammer all have in common? Welcome to the world of looksmaxxers. Let’s start at the beginning.” Mark Sanders introduces a concerning trend for young men and offers a much more satisfying hope. Here Are the Lessons I’ve Learned About Single Missionaries (From a Lifetime of Being One). I’m neither single nor a missionary, but still very much appreciate Andy Smith’s thoughts on the matter. “I always assumed that I would get married. I never thought I would enter full-time ministry. Yet, here I am, a contented single missionary since 1989.” Don’t Be Afraid to Provoke Your Brothers. Michael Kelley says why it’s important that we provoke one another. “I grew up in a house with two brothers. By the time we were all in school, ‘provoking’ was down to an art form. For each of my brothers, I knew the right buttons to push to get a rise out of them. I knew the words, the facial expressions, or even the subtle hint to drop that would flush their anger. What’s more, I knew how to do it to one of them to get at the other one. Like I said, an art form.” On Wesley Huff All those who have heard the recent news about Wesley Huff’s plagiarism have been shocked by it, myself no less than anyone else. I think Glen Scrivener is especially helpful, firm, and compassionate in this video . Even if you don’t watch it all, consider watching the final 10 minutes for the brief “sermon” he preaches there. Huff released a statement yesterday, which you can read on X or Facebook . Flashback The Blessing of a Higher Purpose in Our Pain. The chief end of affliction is to glorify God and enjoy him. The purpose of our lives is the purpose of our times of struggle, loss, grief, illness, and bereavement. The local church enables the world to look upon the canvas of God’s people and see an authentic painting of Christ’s love and holiness, not a forgery. —Jonathan Leeman Download Share See Also A La Carte (April 1) A L

content: I have been blogging at Challies.com on a daily basis for over 23 years now. That long commitment has allowed me to write thousands of articles and hundreds of book reviews while also sending millions of visitors to other sites through the daily A La Carte feature. Though I’ve also written a number of books, the blog has always remained the “main thing.” Much of the blog’s content is now also translated into Spanish , French , and a number of other languages. One of my great desires has always been to freely give away as much as possible. I intend for it to always remain entirely free for all who visit . While, for obvious reasons, this can’t happen when it comes to books, I’ve made it my goal to ensure that everything else has been freely and widely distributed. While this has been possible largely because of advertisers, there is also a key role for the generosity of individuals. This is where patrons come in—patrons like you. There are a couple of different options for you to consider. The first is recurring monthly gifts. A service called Patreon provides a convenient means of linking content producers (like me) with ongoing supporters (like you). You can learn more and sign up at Patreon.com/challies . I also share monthly ministry and family updates there. The second is one-time gifts. If that is of interest to you, they can be made electronically via PayPal . If you prefer to send a one-time gift via check, you can simply mail a check (drawn on a US or Canadian bank) to this address: Tim Challies 1011 Upper Middle Road East, Box #1214 Oakville, Ontario L6H 5Z9 Canada Funds donated will be used to support my family and to help create great content or to otherwise improve, support, and enhance Challies.com. In one way or another, they will all be used to allow me to continue to do what I have been doing for these past 23+ years. Please understand that I intend for Challies.com to always remain entirely free. In fact, patrons help ensure that it always remains that way. Thank you for considering becoming a patron of Challies.com. Your support means so much to me. And this is the end of my once-yearly mention of this subject! title: A La Carte (November 19)
summary: The hardest day you may ever face / For the ones like me / Praying to the God who rules history / Dear Gen Alpha, Claude wants to turn you into a toad / Old dogs and new tricks / Getting a handle on our emotions / Kindle deals and more See Also A La Carte (April 24) A La Carte (November 27) A La Carte (November 22)
content: Thanks for reading A La Carte! I’ve got a good collection of articles, sales, deals, and other material for you this morning. I hope you enjoy it! Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a new edition of John Piper’s Desiring God , two reader-friendly studies in Romans from Tim Keller, The Gospel After Christendom , and my own From the Rising of the Sun (which, to remind you, includes the full documentary for free). Westminster Books is featuring my three Goers books for kids, each of which features a well-known Christian figure. They are nicely discounted. Logos users will want to check out Bible Study Week where you’ll find lots of deals, highlighted by the Tyndale OT & NT Commentaries at $4.99 each. Recommended Reading The Hardest Day You May Ever Face. This is a beautifully tragic piece of writing from Kimberly Wagner as she recounts an extremely hard day. “Daylight was just breaking over the ridge beyond the hills when I slipped into Mom’s bedroom and climbed into the bed beside her, the same bed that as a child I’d run to in the middle of the night to find safety and comfort. On this date, many years ago, we laid my dad’s body in the grave. But, Momma no longer remembers dates, or only guesses to know what season of the year we’re in. She won’t know the significance of today’s date, but she does have a foggy awareness that, to her today represents something terrible on her horizon.” For the Ones Like Me. Zachary Conover writes for those who are like him in that they were raised as good church kids. “What does it mean that we were dead in our trespasses and sins? How were we enemies of God? How were our hearts in rebellion against His Word? For students who have grown up attending church, reading the Bible, and learning about Jesus, these descriptions can be difficult to reconcile with their own experience. I understand that difficulty because I was one of those kids.” Praying to the God Who Rules History. Casey McCall reminds us that when we pray, we pray to the God who rules history. “If your doctrine of God leads you to pray less, you need to reevaluate your understanding of God. If your system of theology leads you to underemphasize the practical power of petitionary prayer in your life, you need to modify your system.” Dear Gen Alpha, Claude Wants to Turn You Into a Toad. Please, for the Love of All Things Human, Don’t Let It. Christina Bieber Lake warns members of Gen Alpha about what an all-out and unthoughtful commitment to Claude and other AI apps is likely to do to them. “In simple terms, we are moving from AI (Artificial Intelligence), which is about getting help processing information, to AGI (Artificial General Intelligence), which is about telling a machine what to do and letting it do it while you sit back and file your fingernails. Experts are saying that AGI will produce ten times the impact of the industrial revolution at ten times the speed.” Old Dogs and New Tricks. “I’m not opposed to the idea of people retiring after many decades of work. They have worked hard, so why not enjoy the fruit of their labor? But what I’ve found disquieting is the static nature that characterizes some retirements. I’ve seen some light, however, at the end of the tunnel and from where I stand, it doesn’t look like a train!” J.V. Fesko explains why he isn’t eager to retire, even if he does eventually withdraw from the front lines of work. Getting a Handle on Our Emotions. Writing for the Biblical Counseling Coalition, Esther St. John offers counsel on getting a handle on emotions, or, perhaps better said, stewarding them faithfully. A Great Error Respecting Duty I have often pointed out that Christians used to speak of duty far more often than we do today, since it was important to express and fulfill the duties God had given his people. You can read what William Plumer believed about duty in this brief quote from one of his works, A Word to the Weary . God’s people sometimes fall into a great error respecting their duty.

title: What Takes 20 Years to Build Takes 5 Minutes to Destroy
summary: I think we’ve all heard many variations of the adage, “It takes 20 years to build a reputation, but only five minutes to destroy it.” A good name that has been established through many years of honor, success, or skilled leadership can be ruined in a moment when an act of immorality comes to light. See Also A La Carte (2/13) The Sinner’s Opinion of Himself The True Character of Unbelief
content: I think we’ve all heard many variations of the adage, “It takes 20 years to build a reputation, but only five minutes to destroy it.” A good name that has been established through many years of honor, success, or skilled leadership can be ruined in a moment when an act of immorality comes to light. Until a couple of weeks ago, Jensen Huang seemed to be on top of the world. While Nvidia, the company he co-founded, had long been a Silicon Valley success story, the rise of AI had driven it to new heights of success and its CEO to new heights of prosperity. Nvidia became the most valuable company in the world, its market capitalization of nearly $6 trillion surpassing even Apple’s. Huang’s net worth soared to over $200 billion, making him one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the richest men in history. His two children have advanced positions within the company and his wife of more than 40 years distributes vast sums of money through their charitable foundation. Huang carefully curated his reputation and, as is so often the case in Silicon Valley, his image, with his slick black leather jackets becoming his trademark. Today, of course, Huang is no longer CEO of Nvidia or anything else. He was forced to resign after it came to light that he had engaged in extramarital affairs with multiple women, one of whom is allegedly a Chinese spy and another of whom is reportedly a subordinate within Nvidia. His image was shattered in a moment, and his reputation is now in tatters. The company lost over half a trillion dollars of value in the aftermath—value that was subtracted from Huang’s wealth, of course, but also from that of everyday investors whose wealth is far more modest. Pictures of his wife and children were splashed all over the news, and stories about his exploits were printed in every major media outlet in the world. The harm to his reputation is beyond repair, yet must pale in comparison to the harm and shame he has brought to his family. I hope that as Huang ponders what has become of his life, he has the wisdom to ask this: was it worth it? I hope each one of us asks the same, for Huang is not the first person to be tempted to grave sin , nor the first to succumb to temptation. In different ways and to different degrees, that is a battle we all fight every day. I have no experience of committing adultery, but I understand that it is exhilarating, and that doing what is forbidden delivers a great rush. And I suppose it must be exhilarating, for why else would a person risk so much to pursue it? Why else would a person do something that so defies common sense? Why else would a person gamble everything for the sake of illicit, fleeting pleasures? News reports describe him, in his final days at the company, calling himself “a piece of [expletive].” And while I wouldn’t phrase it that way, he’s not wrong that this situation has exposed him as what he truly is, and it’s actually far worse than the way he describes it. I might choose the word “wretch” to describe him, and not just him, but all of us. We are all wretches, for we are all wretched, people who trade short-term pleasure for long-term pain and fleeting joys for enduring sorrows. Sin makes us act like madmen, for sin is madness. And it leaves us wretched—desperately unhappy and in the sorriest of states. There has never been a sin that was more wise than foolish. There has never been a sin that delivered more gratification than the satisfaction of obedience. There has never been a sin that was worth more than the honor of a good name and an upstanding reputation. Thankfully, there has never been a sin that is beyond Jesus’s capacity to forgive. Though time and again we, like Huang, succumb to temptation, time and again Jesus forgives those who humble themselves before him to confess their sin and ask his forgiveness. May we all have the wisdom to see ourselves in Huang and to see in him a vivid example of the reality that sin promises joy while delivering sorr

title: How to Beat Scrupulosity
summary: Scrupulosity questions whether we’ve done enough to please God. Pastor John offers a strategy for resisting intrusive thoughts and trusting Christ’s blood. Listen Now
content: Audio Transcript Welcome back to the podcast on this Thanksgiving week. Yesterday, we read about Jesus washing the feet of his disciples in John 13. Jesus worked his basin of water from disciple to disciple on the floor. When he reached Peter, Peter instinctively pulled his feet back and said, “You shall never wash my feet.” Then “Jesus answered him, ‘If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.’ Simon Peter said to him, ‘Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!’” Dump the basin on my head. Give me a shower! And then “Jesus said to him, ‘The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean’” (John 13:8–10). Peter is clean. He was chosen, and he was redeemed. Christ’s future work has already applied to him. Now he only needs his feet washed. Confessing sin is a part of daily cleansing (1 John 1:9), and that practice is never inconsistent with being “completely clean.” Peter is a living metaphor for justification and sanctification. And it tells me we can miss what Christ has done for us because we have dirt on our feet. We fixate on washing off the dust every day. We obsess over daily sanctification and forget that Christ washed us clean. Today on Ask Pastor John: how to beat scrupulosity. Today’s question is from a middle-aged man named Dave. “Pastor John, thank you for taking my question. I have struggled for many years with scrupulosity. That’s the word I learned last week while watching YouTube videos. When I looked up that word, scrupulosity, I wept for joy. My obsessive fears have destroyed my peace for many years. And I think I have discovered the root of most of my spiritual challenges and struggle with anxiety. So, now I want to ask you, Pastor John, what advice would you give to a man who has for years been paralyzed by scrupulosity?” There is a similarity between ordinary spiritual attacks that every believer endures, on the one hand, and more sustained obsessions that some believers endure, on the other hand. There’s a similarity. There’s an overlap. In other words, I don’t think we should overstate or understate the peculiar seriousness of what it is to deal with scrupulosity, or what is sometimes called obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Let me try to illustrate what I mean by the overlap between (1) the normal threat of a thought or an image or a behavior becoming an obsession that all of us experience and (2) the more persistent thoughts or images or behaviors that keep returning and returning, and won’t let a person have any rest, like a tick that bites you on the leg and sinks into your skin, and you try to pull it off, but it just grabs on deeper and harder. All of us deal with this danger. I’ve dealt with it personally and written about it, mostly in relation to sexual threats. For example, you inadvertently see some sexually riveting situation — say, a couple having sex on the ground behind your garage. Immediately, that image lodges itself in your consciousness with tremendous force. It threatens to take over. It wants to stay there and be developed in living color by your imagination. You can adapt this situation, this sexual temptation, to whatever your temptation is, whatever the threat of repetition is. You know the kind of thing I’m talking about. What do you do? Here’s my strategy. I’ll just sum it up quickly and then show how it might apply to this issue of scrupulosity. ANTHEM is my technique for handling a situation of threatening preoccupation with thoughts that ought not to be in my head. A: Avoid what triggers the thought or the image. If it’s inadvertent, don’t look back. If you can avoid the trigger in the first place, avoid it. N: Say no out loud to Satan, to your own mind. No — a strong, decisive no. “You will not have dominion over me (Romans 6:14)!” No to that thought, image, or memory. T: Turn your mind to another compelling reality. It might be the bloody body of Jesus hanging on the cross to make you pure. It m

title: Can’t You Just Do Something New?

content: How often does church-leadership content online reveal a lightly veiled obsession with new ? The experts today might not come out and say it, but the assumption often seems to be: Surely after two thousand years and all of our light-year advances in technology, the church needs a serious upgrade. Capturing this sentiment, one article insists, “Church leaders face two options. Either battle the marketplace currents and strive to convince enough people to pay for sermon-centric Sunday gatherings, or rethink that model to better fit the realities of making disciples in the twenty-first century.” Someone recently shared a clip with me that illustrates one such updated model. The video features a popular preacher who begins his Sunday sermon by driving a Rolls-Royce onto a stage. Twenty-two screens surround him, and hundreds of light bulbs hang overhead. The “preacher” steps out of the half-a-million-dollar car and takes critics like me head-on: There are some of you who are saying, “Oh man, I can’t believe you drove a Rolls-Royce into church. Man, that’s gimmicky.” No, it’s not; it’s godly. “Oh, that’s trite. That’s flippant.” No, it’s from Christ’s playbook. If you ever go to church and you find yourself bored, blame the communicator, the pastor. Don’t blame God. Yeah, for some reason we go to church and expect boredom. Just the opposite should be true. We are — and this is going to mess you up — we are in the entertainment business. I agree that no one should be bored in church — and I certainly agree that God is not to blame for any boredom in the pews. This preacher’s gimmick implies, however, that the same old formula for church — prayer, singing, fellowship, preaching — can’t possibly keep the attention of modern people like you. Mere sermons won’t cut it. God needs us to spice things up. God is not surprised by our state-of-the-art technology or shriveling attention spans, and he has told us, from the beginning, what captures souls when we gather for worship. He’s told us how to do church, and his counsel hasn’t expired. A Church Anyone Would Want Do you want to hear about a church that was emphatically not bored? They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. And awe came upon every soul , and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common. And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved. (Acts 2:42–47) Don’t you want to be a part of a church like that? Don’t you want your local church to taste the camaraderie, sacrifice, growth, and joy these people experienced when they gathered? The God-authored recipe is remarkably simple and durable: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” What did this church do when it grew so wildly and unexpectedly? They gathered. They ate. They gave. They prayed. They preached. And because they devoted themselves to God’s inspired Sunday-service plan, they rejoiced and their numbers multiplied. It’s dumbfounding that we see this kind of church thrive for literally millennia and still conclude it’s time to shake things up. “Sunday sermons got us this far,” we say, “but we’ll take it from here.” What if God knew everything we know — artificial intelligence, fiber-optic internet, driverless cars, those new robot vacuums that can clean stairs — and deliberately told churches to pray, sing, eat, drink, and preach the word anyway? Preaching to Itching Ears God knew exactly what changes and pressures our churches would face in the twenty-first century, and so he warned us t

title: You Really Can Know Jesus
summary: Can we really know Jesus Christ? He may be high and lifted up, but seven fundamental truths make ongoing access to him possible. Watch Now
content: I have looked forward to this conference on “Knowing Jesus.” That theme is both awesome and scary. Awesome because, does it get any better than this? Knowing Jesus is at the very heart of reality, why we exist, why God made the world, what “education in serious joy” is for, what the gospel is for us. (“There is no greater thing,” as Graham Kendrick wrote in the song “Knowing Jesus” in 1993.) But it also could be scary because knowing Jesus is personal and spiritual-relational and enigmatic. We might think we know him until we pause and ask this: What does it mean to know Jesus? What’s it like? Do I really know him? I can imagine a few general orientations in this room. One group says, “I love Jesus. I know him; I commune with him regularly, even daily. Knowing and enjoying him is my life and joy. And oh, do I want to know him more! Any help I can get this weekend in sweetening my knowing and walking with Jesus, I’ll take it.” Another group says, “I think I know him. I say I know him. But do I really? I know about him. I’m in a church community where people talk freely about ‘knowing Jesus.’ But what really do they mean by this? How do you know someone you’ve never been in the same room with? How do you know someone if you’ve never seen their physical face and heard their physical voice or interacted with them in the way you do with a spouse or best friend? I think I know him, but I want to really know him — and know that I know him — and more often and more deeply enjoy the wonder of communing with him.” Then, a last group says, “I don’t know him. I know people who say they do, but I wonder, Do they? And whether they do or not, I don’t. If someone asked me, ‘Do you know Jesus?’ I would have to say, ‘I know some things about him, but I don’t know him, not like persons know persons.’” Some in this last category might even say, “I’m a Christian. I follow Jesus. I profess faith in Jesus. But if ‘knowing Jesus’ means anything like what it means to know other persons, then if I’m being honest, no, I don’t know him.” Our hope this weekend is that this theme and these four messages (and our concluding panel) have something to offer to each of these groups. And since our theme is “Knowing Jesus,” perhaps the greatest theme of all, my hope is that this weekend might truly be life-changing for you (whatever group you’re in), that something significant might be in the offing for your soul. And that some in this room would say, “I came in Friday morning knowing about Jesus, but not knowing Jesus. But now I know him.” Or: “Now I see in a whole new way what it means to know the risen Christ and walk with him.” I believe that, given this theme, today and tomorrow could make for a whole new day, a new era, in your life, and I want to begin our time by asking God for that. Father in heaven, be pleased to do that this weekend in this room. We don’t want to just know about Jesus. We want to know Jesus, and enjoy him, and have our souls and lives changed and shaped and directed and energized by him. Father, for those in this room who genuinely know your Son, make this weekend an occasion for knowing him more and going deeper with him. And for those who don’t know him, or know that they know him, make this a day of decisive change. We own that knowing your Son is not an achievement to be secured. It is a gift of your immeasurable grace to be humbly and gladly received. Open our minds and hearts to receive the offer of your outstretched hand in Jesus. Oh, may we know him and supremely enjoy him, and may it change everything for us. In Jesus’s name we pray. Amen. Where is Jesus right now? He’s not here. Not in body. There is a critical sense in which he is here in Spirit; we’ll come to that. But let me begin by recognizing the problem (so to speak) for knowing Jesus created by his ascension. Jesus was here. He dwelled among us. He taught and discipled. He died and rose. But now he’s not presently among us and physically accessible as he was for his d

content: When I turned forty, YouTube decided my body needed help — desperately. Advertisements regularly shouted warnings about my sagging arms, the creases etched into the corners of my eyes, and the coarse texture of my hair. Marketers promised products to smooth away my wrinkles, brighten my complexion, and shrink my soft midsection, all for the nominal sum of $24.95 a month. At first, I just rolled my eyes and groaned at these messages. But with each creak of my knees and new splotch on my face, the insecurities such ads churned up took root and burrowed deep. Perhaps I should cover my salt-and-pepper strands with boxed dye , I wondered. All the while, the onslaught of imperatives continued: Soften. Polish. Gloss. Tighten. Defy. Reverse. Godly Vision Such verbs don’t appear in the Bible. Scripture teaches us that “gray hair is a crown of glory” rather than something to moisturize, color, and conceal at all costs (Proverbs 16:31). But when social media scrutinizes our granny knees and wobbly bits, that picture of glory seems as elusive as the stamina we once enjoyed in our twenties. To be clear, the Bible doesn’t prohibit cosmetics or remedies. God clothes even the lilies of the field in beauty (Luke 12:27), and in his mercy, he provides medicine to relieve our pains (1 Timothy 5:23). But Scripture also teaches that our relationship with God far outweighs the transient beauty of shiny hair and supple skin. “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the L ORD is to be praised,” we read in Proverbs 31:30. As we age, how do we calibrate our vision to God’s? How do we look into the mirror, perceive every crevice, laugh-line, and blotch, and then respond with deeper joy in the one whose mercy has granted us every year and silvery strand? Sisters, here are four ways to view our changing appearance through the lens of heaven. 1. Embrace God’s Sovereign Design The world tells us our aging bodies are a problem to fix. Researchers expect the global anti-aging cosmetics market to exceed $90 billion within the next five years. The products driving this boom could stock a chemistry laboratory: retinoids, peptides, hyaluronic acid, niacinamide extracts, and ultraviolet light. Moisturizing and pigmenting aren’t enough; now, we need to restore the skin itself, halt cells in their decay, and command unraveling proteins to coil. Ironically, God engineers the very dimples and folds this multibillion-dollar industry seeks to abolish. Had our predecessors in the garden loved him with all their heart, soul, mind, and strength (Mark 12:30), anti-aging serums would reap zero profit. Our bodies, untouched by sin, would work, rest, nurture, and rejoice for all eternity without a single wayward hair or troublesome mole to concern us. But aging — the slow descent into physical death — is part of our God-given wages of rebellion (Romans 6:23). God has decreed that our return to the dust will involve thinning bones and aching backs (Genesis 3:17–19). Our hearts, pumping over a hundred thousand times each day, will thicken under the toil of prolonged service. Our muscles will melt away, and our joints will stiffen and throb. Our crooked backs and rotten teeth aren’t a cause for celebration, but the one who rules over them is. The Maker of heaven and earth is sovereign over every lax fiber and withered cell (Proverbs 16:4; Psalm 103:19). No molecule, protein, or cell spins outside of his control. When we consider God’s sovereign design behind every crevice and pockmark, we remember that he holds us in the palm of his hand (Psalm 31:15; Isaiah 49:16). For those who know Christ, there is no safer, more privileged place to be. 2. Remember Your Fleeting Nature Gray hair alerts us to our limited time on this earth. Apart from Christ, such reminders terrify, as they warn of the day when kings and beggars alike will plead for the mountains to hide them from judgment (Revelation 6:15–17). With the end in view, the world’s mad scramble to reverse aging

content: It’s feasting season. Thanksgiving. Advent. New Year’s. But for Americans in particular, is there such a thing as a non -feasting season? Our society has a bizarre love-hate relationship with food, pulling the plate toward us with one hand while pushing it away with the other. On the one hand, about 40 percent of adults are clinically obese; on the other, more than one in eight adults rely on GLP-1 to suppress their appetite. We want food and we want to want food less. We struggle to break free from the clutches of Big Food, so we look to Big Pharma for help. Happy Thanksgiving? What’s the remedy for this gastronomic schizophrenia? As counterintuitive as it sounds, godly feasting provides an antidote to foolish gluttony. Feasting vs. Feeding The Bible has a lot to say about food, not just in isolated verses but in plot points central to the arc of Scripture. Many of the most egregious sins centered on food. For instance, the first sin involved rebellious eating, looking to something forbidden in search of goodness (Genesis 3:6). After the exodus, Israel grumbled about their desire for Pharaoh’s pots of meat (Exodus 16:3). Then, when the Lord provided manna in the wilderness, Israel reenacted the sin of Eve when they gathered food on the Sabbath against God’s command (Exodus 16:27–30). But the Bible also commends feasting, both spiritual and physical. Jesus offers himself as the bread of life, given for the nourishment of the saints in exile (John 6:35). And the church looks forward to a meal at the consummation of history, the marriage feast of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Between the resurrection and return of the Lamb, we weekly feast on his body and blood, anchoring our minds on what Christ has done and what Christ will do (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). Godly feasting leans into our place in between the times by remembering with gratitude what was and anticipating with joy what will be. All the blessed feasts in the Scriptures are communal celebrations . Something extraordinary has happened; raise a glass to the King! We shouldn’t eat what we regularly eat today; instead, “bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found!” (Luke 15:23–24). We break from feeding ourselves (simply giving our body what it needs) in order to feast (eating and drinking more than we need) as a blessed means of joyously celebrating the work of God in history. But most Christians rarely, if ever, truly feast with mindful gratitude. We just overeat. Spiritual Malnutrition “A companion of gluttons shames his father” (Proverbs 28:7). The glutton does not feast; his god is his belly. He looks for deliverance in his next snack, his next meal, his next drink. He does not fully grasp that man does not live by bread alone. He is not marked by gratitude. The emptiness in his soul, the purposelessness of his life, and the joylessness of his ease have taken root as a spiritual disease. “A glutton is one who raids the icebox for a cure for spiritual malnutrition,” Frederick Buechner observed ( Wishful Thinking , 35). Americans, overall, remain locked in a permanent state of pseudo-feasting. Our culture combines industrial-grade, highly addictive food products and dopamine-seeking, nihilistic joylessness. We mindlessly munch. Often, we hardly even taste or enjoy our food. (A 2026 JAMA study revealed 69 percent of kids and 78 percent of adults use screens while eating.) This is an often-undiscussed problem within the church. I don’t know any Christians who intend to be gluttonous. But I know many, myself included, who have at times felt buried by the shame that follows an episode or season marked by a lack of self-control. We know we cannot make peace with sin, but we aren’t sure what this specific path of repentance looks like. So, when believers recognize the shameful pattern, we try to restrict our calories or go on a diet, which doesn’t stick. We purge and we binge — godless,

title: Are My Prayers Selfish?
summary: How do we know if we’re praying according to God’s will? Pastor John distinguishes unfaithful, selfish prayer from God-honoring, faithful prayer. Listen Now
content: Audio Transcript If we transcribed our prayers from the last year and shared them with each other, what would be obvious? Would it show lofty prayers for the nations? Would we be found praying most often that God’s name be hallowed on earth? Or would we see in those transcripts a lot of self-centered prayers that constantly revolve around our daily needs? And if that was what we found, would that really be a problem? As we will read in our Bible reading, 1 John 5 tells us that if we ask for anything according to God’s will, he will hear us. Today on Ask Pastor John: Are my prayers too selfish? It’s the question on the mind of Bridget. She’s a college student at UMass Amherst. “Pastor John, hello, and thank you for the Ask Pastor John podcast. I’ve been thinking a lot about this question of prayer. In 1 John 5:14–15,” in our reading tomorrow, “we receive the great promise that if we ask for anything according to God’s will, he hears and answers us. First Peter 5:7 welcomes us to cast all our cares on him. But then James 4:3 warns us that prayers driven by selfish motives won’t be answered. “I’m trying to fit these texts together in practice. We are encouraged to bring all our cares to God, so I get confused about how much we need to pre-align them with his will before we even speak them. Are we truly free to pray for anything, or are we only supposed to pray for certain cares? What I’m really trying to figure out is this: before I start praying for something specific I really want, how can I know if my desire is in line with God’s will or if the desire is selfish?” Maybe digging into the context of James 4:3, which Bridget refers to, might shed light on how to know if our motivations are pleasing to God when we come to him in prayer. It’s surprising, even shocking imagery that we find here in James 4:1–5. Listen: “You do not have, because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly.” Now, that’s the question: What’s “wrongly”? What is it to pray badly? “To spend it on your passions. You [adulteresses]!” Now, the translation “adulteresses” is important. It is plain, straightforward, and feminine (moichalides). To translate it “adulterous people” doesn’t help us. It is feminine, and it is “adulteresses,” and the image being created is crucial, and you can’t see it without the word adulteresses: “You adulteresses.” There are people in this church who are acting like adulteresses. They are acting like they belong to God as their husband while they’re acting like an unfaithful wife. “Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?” That is, a wife who goes after other lovers (namely, the world) is going to make her husband angry — justifiably jealous (namely, God). “Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world,” the paramour down the hall, “makes himself an enemy of God,” the jilted husband. “Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, ‘He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us’?” That’s what a good husband does. A good husband feels indignant and has a deep sense of, “You’re mine. You shouldn’t give yourself to another man.” “Selfishness is when you want something and you’re going to seek it whether it dishonors God or not.” So, we’re talking about prayer. We’re talking about prayer in this paragraph. And James is saying there is a kind of prayer that treats God like a cuckold. It refers to a husband whose wife is cheating on him. That’s a cuckold. Christians are making God into a cuckold. How? When it says they are praying just to spend it on their passions. The picture is of an unfaithful wife who asked her husband for $50 so she can go down the hall and pay another man to have sex with her. That’s the picture. She’s using prayer to cheat on her husband, God. How does that help us answer the question of how to sort out whether we are praying in accord with God’s will or being selfish? content: “Hold the lettuce.” The simple sentence, perhaps stated more frequently than we might hope, captures a crucial hallmark that predominates in the thinking of many. At a recent lunch with a friend, I saw this firsthand. For my friend, it wasn’t just the lettuce. The instructions he gave restrained the cook from adding anything remotely vegetable-like to the hamburger. Notwithstanding my jibe, my friend held fast to his decision. He was the one ordering. And he expected (rightly so!) to be served what he desired. After all, the customer is king. This cluster of expectations animates the modern marketplace. We want products tailored to our specific needs. We seek out services that let us pay only for what we want. We get frustrated when we take the car to a mechanic who not only fixes the problem we knew about but also takes the liberty of repairing other problems (and charging liberally for them). In short, we want (and expect) to be served according to our preferences and felt needs. Innocuous enough when it comes to the morsels on our plates, the reign of personal preferences involves more serious implications when it extends over the rest of life. And in the life of faith, the consequences are serious indeed. For preference-driven faith will, in the end, produce a Christless Christianity. Have It Your Way What do we hope for when we join the church for worship? Parsing motives presents no easy project, especially if there are children in tow or responsibilities for some aspect of the service or fellowship. Few of us have the personal or cognitive space to search out the depths of our hearts en route to the Sunday morning service. But the way home often presents opportunities to interrogate those hidden recesses. The questions we pose shed light on what is in our hearts: “How did you like the sermon this morning?” “Didn’t the worship team nail it today?” We tend to ask not about a confrontation with gospel truth but about measures of personal satisfaction. If our questions begin illuminating this tendency, the answers we give put our motives on clear display: “I thought the pastor did a great job! I really liked . . .” or “Ya know, I just wasn’t feeling it this morning; the sermon didn’t really speak to me.” “Yes, the worship was great!” or “I thought the team was a bit off. Did you hear them mess up on that one song?” So often, whether at the sandwich shop or on the way home from church, preference-driven language bubbles out of our mouths like boiling water from an unwatched pot. For many, our post-service concerns center far too frequently on how well certain aspects of the service met our felt needs. What did I gain from the sermon? Did I enjoy the music? Service to the ascendant self predominates. We reflect on the worship gathering in a manner unsettlingly similar to how we might reflect on a hamburger: It was decent, but I’ve had better elsewhere. I think they overdid the mayonnaise, and I would have preferred sesame rather than a brioche bun. Whether we want to admit it or not, our expectations of being served as we please spill into our perceived relationship to the church’s gathered worship. Those same expectations shape how we approach our Lord. We tend naturally, in our sin, to want merely an affirming savior. We like to hear that Jesus loves sinners so much that he died to win them, for hearing this affirms that our need for forgiveness has been met. We like to hear that his love for his sheep never falters, for hearing this quells the fear that perhaps our snide words or dubious choices or the train wreck of our inner thoughts might put our hope in jeopardy. We like to hear how our Lord railed against the hypocrisy and legalism of the Pharisees, for hearing this makes us smile inwardly, pleased that we are not so pretentious and uptight. Messages such as these leave us content, unruffled, ready to carry on with life as normal, affirmed in our preferred way of life by a (truncated) gospel that accomplishes little b
author: Seth Porch

title: ‘Only the beginning’ for IMB ministry partner in South Asia
summary: The conversation began on a dusty road in rural South Asia. Siraj, a Christian, told Derrick Waters about his desire to share the gospel with Muslims. How could he begin discussions about Christ with his neighbors? After months of training and encouragement, Siraj said, “I will soon share the gospel with 100 Muslims. I know that at least a few will believe.” Waters and his wife, Rosemary, are International Mission Board missionaries who serve in South Asia. His connection with Siraj is a breakth
content: IMB missionary Derrick Waters spent many days in areas like this market, learning his mission field. He made a breakthrough when he met Siraj, who now confidently shares the gospel. IMB Photo The conversation began on a dusty road in rural South Asia. Siraj, a Christian, told Derrick Waters about his desire to share the gospel with Muslims. How could he begin discussions about Christ with his neighbors? After months of training and encouragement, Siraj said, “I will soon share the gospel with 100 Muslims. I know that at least a few will believe.” Waters and his wife, Rosemary, are International Mission Board missionaries who serve in South Asia. His connection with Siraj is a breakthrough in sharing the gospel in this strongly Muslim region. When he first arrived on the mission field, Waters spent his early days getting acclimated to his new community by riding on the back of a motorcycle with a national partner, traveling around and making contacts. “My partner was trying to convince me not to buy a helmet because he said he was a safe driver,” Waters said, though he chose to wear the headgear. “It’s a good thing I wore the helmet because he drove into the back of a truck with a metal bar hanging out that smacked my head.” Surviving the motorcycle ride led to the relational network that eventually allowed Waters to meet Siraj. After they connected, Siraj introduced Waters to Muslim friends and watched him share the gospel. “At first, that’s how it was with Siraj,” Waters said. “But what I really wanted was for him to get involved in the work himself.” A few months later, Waters and local ministry partners traveled to Siraj’s village to lead evangelism training. They discussed God’s love for all people, learned key vocabulary and practiced a straightforward way to share personal testimonies and the story of Jesus. Then came the hard part. Waters began asking Siraj to lead conversations. Siraj stumbled through explanations and searched for the right words. He sprinkled in newly learned terms and nervously worked through the gospel message. Slowly, confidence replaced fear. After another season of ministry together, Siraj told Waters something he would never forget. “Before you came, I didn’t know how to share the gospel with Muslims,” Siraj said. “I wanted to, but I didn’t know how. Now I feel like I can do it.” The transformation became visible during a gathering arranged by a local teacher. Dozens of parents assembled to listen. Siraj stood before them, visibly nervous. His first few sentences faltered. He started, stopped and restarted. Then, something changed. Finding his rhythm, he shared what he had learned, speaking clearly and naturally. He used the vocabulary he had practiced and explained the message of Jesus with growing confidence. By the end of the meeting, the listeners invited the believers to pray for sick family members. They served snacks and chai, thanked them for coming and invited them back. For Waters, it was a glimpse of what God could do through one willing believer. Today, Siraj continues learning and sharing. He studies from a Bible in the local language that helps him engage more effectively with Muslim friends. He distributes Bibles, shares the gospel with coworkers and regularly speaks with people in the villages. This house is part of the village where Siraj lives with his wife, three daughters and his mother. He supports them on the equivalent of US$4 a day, while also farming his land and studying to earn his Ph.D. IMB Photo His enthusiasm is especially remarkable considering his circumstances. Siraj supports his wife, three daughters and his mother on the equivalent of US$4 a day. He farms a small plot of land and studies for exams in hopes of pursuing a Ph.D.  Despite these responsibilities, he continues making time to tell others about Christ. title: A Thanksgiving in Poland to remember
summary: For Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their family, Thanksgiving is more than a cherished American holiday. Living and serving in Poland as International Mission Board missionaries, it has become one of their most effective opportunities to build relationships, share their culture and ultimately point people to Christ. While Poland celebrates Christmas and Easter on a grand scale, Thanksgiving is uniquely American. Many Poles are familiar with the holiday and curious about its traditions. Over the years,
content: In 2018, God provided food for more than 70 people, double the expected number, at a Thanksgiving celebration Cal and Erin Hiebsch helped to host in order to share the gospel by telling the story of God’s provision for the Pilgrims on the first Thanksgiving. IMB Photo For Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their family, Thanksgiving is more than a cherished American holiday. Living and serving in Poland as International Mission Board missionaries, it has become one of their most effective opportunities to build relationships, share their culture and ultimately point people to Christ. While Poland celebrates Christmas and Easter on a grand scale, Thanksgiving is uniquely American. Many Poles are familiar with the holiday and curious about its traditions. Over the years, the Hiebsch family has learned to use that curiosity as a bridge for ministry. “Thanksgiving is probably one of our bigger entrées into American culture,” Cal explained. Each year, they invite friends, neighbors and participants from their English conversation clubs to experience a traditional Thanksgiving meal. For many guests, this is their first encounter with foods such as stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potato casserole and roasted turkey. Even finding a whole turkey in Poland can be a challenge, since stores more commonly sell turkey breasts and other cuts rather than the whole bird. One Thanksgiving, in particular, is especially memorable for the family. With the help of volunteers, Erin and the culinary crew carefully planned a special celebration. “We had people in four or five different kitchens across the city cooking,” she said. A generous spread of traditional American dishes filled the tables, and invitations had been extended throughout their community. Based on past events, they expected 20 to 30 people to attend. Erin said they planned for “double batches” of each dish with the intention of everybody trying a little of everything that was served. Servers fill up plates as IMB missionaries Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their friends host a Thanksgiving meal in Poland. They planned for 20 or 30 people to show up, but nearly 70 people filled the house. Thankfully, everyone had a full meal and heard the gospel message. IMB Photo As the evening began, guests kept arriving. More came through the doors. Then more. Soon the room was packed. Instead of the anticipated crowd of a few dozen, nearly 70 people showed up. The gathering became standing-room only. “I quietly asked a couple of the volunteer ladies to be praying that there would be enough for everyone,” Erin recalled. Cal was serving as emcee for the event, welcoming guests and sharing the Thanksgiving story. Meanwhile, others were distributing plate after plate of food. Every time someone entered the room, the challenge seemed to grow. How could the food possibly stretch far enough? Yet somehow, it did. People continued to receive full plates. Everyone ate. Conversations flourished around the tables. “The pumpkin pie was especially popular,” Erin said. Guests learned about the history of Thanksgiving and heard how God had provided for the Pilgrims during difficult circumstances. Most importantly, they heard the gospel woven naturally into the evening’s program. When the event finally concluded, the team compared notes and realized an astonishing experience occurred. “We doubled our crowd and had enough food for everyone to have a good Thanksgiving feast,” Cal recalled. To this day, Cal and Erin still talk about that evening. The experience remains difficult to explain, outside of God’s provision. They prepared for one number of guests and served more than twice as many. Whether miraculous or simply an extraordinary provision, the outcome was undeniable. More people than expected were welcomed, fed and exposed to the hope of Christ. An American holiday became a platform for meaningful conversations and gospel witness in a place far from home.
